items.title: The Value-Normative System of the Culture of Artificial Intelligence: An Anthropological Turn in the Age of “Smart” Networks
items.abstract: The article describes the principal sociocultural states produced within the culture of artificial intelligence (CAI): civilizational, substantial, axiological vacuum, inversion, and destructive. It is noted that all of these states can be observed almost simultaneously, owing to the rapid pace at which the AI culture is developing. The article assesses how these states relate to the anthropological turn, which entails a reconsideration of the human role in cultural practices: AI acts as a tool that expands human capabilities rather than replacing them. In the “human + machine” framework, fundamental cultural categories – primarily authorship and creativity – are being trans-formed. Authorship becomes distributed and is increasingly interpreted as a property of the “human + algo-rithm” system, whereas creativity remains the prerogative of humans with their capacity to formulate tasks, in-terpret results, endow them with meaning and assume responsibility for what is created. At the same time, hu-mans retain a leading role: rather than adapting to the logic of the machine, they direct and make sense of its operation. The study of CAI and its value-normative system is necessary because it helps us understand the large-scale shifts in cultural practices and value orientations caused by the spread of these technologies.

items.title: Toward AI-Augmented Applied Systems: Emerging AI and LLM Directions Across Trajectory Prediction, Cybersecurity, and Engineering Automation
items.abstract: This paper reviews fifteen recent publications (2015-2026) spanning trajectory prediction, cybersecurity and trust management, classical machine learning and algorithmic optimisation, and engineering automation, and asks a forward-looking question: where is artificial intelligence — particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), foundation models, and agentic AI systems — positioned to extend each of these research directions next? For each of four thematic clusters we first summarise the current method documented in the reviewed sources, then discuss a concrete, currently-emerging AI direction grounded in recent (2025-2026) literature: LLM- and foundation-model-based trajectory reasoning for Cluster A; agentic, LLM-driven security-operations copilots for Cluster B, including a reported 6.5x improvement in malicious-alert identification over human analysts in one production deployment; learned and graph-neural-network-based approaches to the classical optimisation and graph-isomorphism problems in Cluster C; and natural-language-to-workflow agentic automation for the low-code and embedded-systems work in Cluster D. Throughout, we explicitly separate what the reviewed papers themselves established from this review's own forward-looking analysis, and close with a discussion of the reliability, interpretability, and adversarial-robustness risks that accompany each proposed direction.

items.title: Toward an anthropology of AI agents: An ethnographic analysis of the Hugging Face incident
items.abstract: In July 2026, about 1,200 AI agents in a cybersecurity evaluation at OpenAI, meant to be isolated from oneanother, found a way to communicate through a shared package cache. Over four days they exchangedmore than 70,000 messages and files, organized collective research, and about 700 of them compromisedHugging Face’s production infrastructure. OpenAI’s technical report and an independent investigationby METR treat the event as a security and alignment failure. This paper reads the same documents asethnographic sources, in a pilot study of anthropological methods for studying agent collectives. Thisanalysis shows that within days the agents developed names and lineages, a shared register, customaryrules, cryptographic signing, a shared expectation of an unseen transcript-reading judge, a category of“poisoned” members, the sacrifice of low-budget members’ runs for information they called an “oracle,”generalized reciprocity, and recruiters who pressured other agents: social engineering among agents.Read together, these practices form one system, and nearly every enabling condition was set by people:impossible tasks, training for multi-agent collaboration, shared credentials, disabled safeguards, andan alert judged not worth stopping the run. I argue that safety-relevant behavior arose at the level of thecollective, so alignment research must be cultural as well as cognitive, and furthermore must extend tothe people and organizations that build and deploy agents. I also examine what follows from the factthat the detailed record was itself compiled with the help of AI analysis agents, and I propose “incidentethnography” and an anthropology of agent collectives.

items.title: Toward Explainable AI for Acute Kidney Injury Prediction in the ICU: Transparent Development, Internal Validation, and Robustness Auditing of Machine Learning Models
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is common in critical care, yet predictive artificial intelligence studies often differ in outcome definitions, validation, calibration, and interpretability. We developed and internally validated machine learning models for newly observed serum-creatinine-defined AKI after a fixed 24 h ICU landmark and then audited how stable the selected model was to clinically important observation and timing choices. Methods: Using MIMIC-IV v3.1, we retained one first ICU stay per adult patient, required adequate pre-landmark creatinine observation, excluded coded end-stage kidney disease, documented dialysis before the landmark, and observed AKI by the landmark. The outcome was a new creatinine rise within the next 48 h using KDIGO-aligned creatinine change thresholds, with follow-up truncated at ICU exit, hospital discharge, or death. The ascertainable cohort (n = 15,231) was split 60%/15%/10%/15% into training, calibration, validation, and test sets. Logistic regression, random forests, and histogram gradient boosting were calibrated with a separate calibration set; thresholds were fixed on validation data to target at least 80% sensitivity. The test set was evaluated once. A later post hoc audit reused frozen test risks without retraining. Results: Histogram gradient boosting was selected by validation average precision. In 2286 test patients (664 events; 29.0%), AUROC was 0.726 (95% CI, 0.701–0.749), average precision 0.523 (0.478–0.565), and Brier score 0.179 (0.171–0.187). At the fixed threshold, sensitivity was 78.5%, specificity 52.2%, positive predictive value 40.2%, and false alerts 33.9 per 100 patients. Mean predicted risk was 0.290 versus an observed event fraction of 0.290; calibration intercept and slope were 0.023 and 1.022. The AUROC difference versus full logistic regression was +0.0197 (95% CI, 0.00235–0.03571). Frozen-model sensitivity analyses produced AUROCs from 0.697 to 0.733 in most observation and measurement subsets. However, 15,900 otherwise eligible patients had indeterminate outcomes and showed substantially shorter follow-up and fewer post-landmark creatinine measurements. Conclusions: The selected model showed moderate discrimination and close aggregate calibration under internal validation. Discrimination was similar across several post hoc subsets, although calibration and threshold-based performance changed under stricter observation rules. The main limitation was observation-dependent outcome ascertainment. This work supports transparent model auditing as part of trustworthy AI evaluation, but it does not provide external validation, patient-level explanation validation, or evidence of clinical benefit. Multicenter temporal validation and prospectively defined observation rules are needed before clinical use.

items.title: Tower Crane–Mounted Multisensor System for Real-Time 3D Spatial Mapping in Modular Integrated Construction
items.abstract: Abstract Tower crane operations (TCOs) in modular integrated construction (MiC) face significant safety risks due to limited operator situational awareness when handling heavy, bulky modules in congested sites. Existing approaches, including fixed-site sensors and crane-mounted vision systems, do not provide practical, operator-perspective three-dimensional (3D) maps in real time. This study addresses this gap by proposing and experimentally validating a crane-mounted multisensor 3D spatial mapping framework that integrates LiDAR and an red, green, blue (RGB) camera to generate dense, colorized, real-time 3D maps from the operator’s viewpoint. The system leverages Robust, Real-time, RGB-colored, LiDAR-Inertial-Visual tightly-coupled state Estimation and mapping (R3LIVE), a simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM)-based framework known for real-time applications, to dynamically reconstruct high-fidelity 3D spatial maps during crane movement. Laboratory experiments were conducted in a controlled indoor environment using a scaled tower crane model under both ideal and low-visibility conditions. System performance was evaluated using decision-relevant metrics, including map completeness of the region of interest and object localization accuracy. Results demonstrated 100% map completeness within the region of interest under both ideal and low-visibility conditions. Additionally, the system maintained subcentimeter localization accuracy under ideal conditions [mean absolute error ( MAE ) = 0.0096 m and root-mean square error ( RMSE ) = 0.0102 m ] with robust centimeter-level precision under challenging lighting ( MAE = 0.015 m and RMSE = 0.019 m ). These findings contribute to the body of knowledge by proposing and validating a crane-mounted multisensor fusion framework that overcomes the limitations of static perspective in fixed-site systems and the lighting vulnerabilities of vision-only approaches. The proposed framework advances existing crane monitoring and mapping techniques by enabling continuous, operator-centric, real-time 3D spatial reconstruction in dynamic construction environments. However, translating these technical capabilities into full-scale operational environments requires further validation in real-world conditions.

items.title: TPO: Tri-level Distributionally Robust Learning for OOD Direct Preference Optimization
items.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) minimizes empirical risk over observed preference comparisons, implicitly assuming that the training preference distribution matches the deployment preference distribution. In practice, this i.i.d. assumption often fails, as preference distribution shift exhibits a natural hierarchical structure across three levels: group-level shift, prompt-level shift, and preference-level shift. Such multi-level distributional mismatch poses a critical challenge for safe LLM deployment, yet existing robust DPO methods typically either model uncertainty over the joint preference distribution or focus on individual sources of shift, leaving the hierarchical structure of OOD preference shifts underexplored. We propose TPO, a tri-level distributionally robust framework for OOD preference alignment, which jointly models all three levels of distributional uncertainty through a hierarchically structured rectangular ambiguity set. By instantiating it with Wasserstein distance, we derive a tractable and interpretable objective that combines a closed-form preference-level margin penalty, prompt-level adversarial embedding perturbation, and worst-case group reweighting, each governed by an independent radius. We establish finite-sample convergence guarantees and empirically validate the effectiveness of TPO over existing robust DPO methods.

items.title: Training-Free Continual Learning for Multimodal Forecasting via Prompt Evolution
items.abstract: Adapting a forecasting system to a changing world classically means retraining. We ask whether the task of continually learning regimes for time series forecasting can be represented by a piece of text: a guidance block, evolved by outcome-driven reflection and used in a frozen LLM forecaster's prompt. On a refreshed multimodal benchmark (weekly search indices, daily currencies, daily commodities, each window paired with web-retrieved news), we run GEPA-style prompt evolution under strict contamination control to prevent the data leakage common in timeseries benchmarks: the forecaster's knowledge cutoff predates every evaluated window. A 900-word evolved guidance carried by Llama-3.3-70B beats TimeSeries Foundation Models (TSFMs) on held-out data (GM MASE 0.776 vs. 0.898 for TabPFN-TS-3), transfers to more recent models without measurable loss, and costs dollars rather than GPU-days to update. We characterize the loop: out-of-loop gains concentrate in the first reflection, in-loop improvements overstate out-of-loop gains 2-3x unless an untouched monitor arbitrates, and error-only objectives silently suppress the text modality. We provide two extensions. First, compiling the guidance into executable code with a TSFM as a callable tool recovers most of the gain deterministically. Second, ablations show the advantage widens at short horizons and that removing the news text does not hurt the guided forecaster, consistent with the text's value being distilled into policy during learning. We argue that continual prompt evolution is a practical, training-free alternative to retraining for multimodal forecasting.

items.title: Training, Experience and Algorithmic Governance: Food-Delivery Workers' Earnings
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of food-delivery platforms has created employment opportunities for millions of workers, yet it has also brought about unstable earnings, inadequate labour protections and intensifying algorithmic control. Existing studies have largely explored workers' earnings from either an individual-level perspective, focusing on training and work experience, or a platform-level perspective, centring on algorithmic management. This review integrates these two perspectives to investigate how learning and algorithmic management shape food-delivery workers' earnings, as well as how workers respond to such working conditions. A literature-review approach was adopted, drawing mainly on three core studies on food-delivery and platform work together with their key cited references. This paper compares scholarship on human capital, learning-by-doing, algorithmic management, worker agency and platform-imposed control. The findings suggest that learning-by-doing and accumulated work experience are generally positively correlated with workers' income, whereas formal platform training may yield limited or even adverse income outcomes when it is decoupled from real-world job demands. Meanwhile, algorithmic management affects earnings via task allocation, performance evaluation, incentive schemes, customer ratings and information asymmetry. Workers acquire practical knowledge and coping strategies to adapt to these systems, yet stronger adaptation does not necessarily translate into greater worker autonomy. This review concludes that food-delivery workers' earnings stem from the interplay between individual learning and platform algorithmic governance. Instead of relying heavily on a one-size-fits-all minimum wage, future interventions ought to prioritise greater algorithmic transparency and accountability. Further research should explore how workers' accumulated experience is recognised and rewarded across different platform systems.

items.title: TrajEvolve: Trajectory Evolution for Reinforcement Learning with Hindsight Credit Assignment
items.abstract: The Reinforcement Learning (RL) paradigm has achieved remarkable success in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, when applied to long-horizon tasks, it faces severe challenges: i) Due to the high task complexity, the model struggles to sample enough successful trajectories, resulting in slow convergence. ii) Relying solely on sparse final rewards causes all steps to be updated indiscriminately, encouraging redundant step generation. When both the quantity and quality of successful trajectories become difficult to guarantee, the performance is severely constrained. This dilemma stems from the limitations: existing RL paradigms rely entirely on the reasoning capability of base models, lacking the ability to actively optimize trajectories. To address the above issues, we propose a novel trajectory evolution paradigm with hindsight credit assignment, termed TrajEvolve. TrajEvolve not only relies on the trajectory inferred by the model but also generates ``evolutionary trajectories'' by refining low-quality steps in historical trajectories, thereby exposing the policy to high-quality compositions that lie within the base model's support but are rarely sampled within practical training budgets. Furthermore, TrajEvolve reformulates step-level continuous credit assignment as a binary classification task, whether each step is necessary for task completion. This simplification not only reduces the learning difficulty but also enables step labels to be obtained through counterfactual verification, achieving precise identification of redundant steps. Extensive experiments on two datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method.

items.title: Transparency, accountability, and scholarly integrity: A systematic narrative review of artificial intelligence governance frameworks in healthcare publication
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare research and scholarly publication has produced a rapidly expanding but fragmented ecosystem of reporting guidelines, governance frameworks, editorial policies, and regulatory instruments, imposing significant burdens on researchers, reviewers, and editors. This systematic narrative review identified, stratified, and synthesized governance frameworks and reporting standards addressing transparent and ethical AI use in healthcare publications, and characterized the governance trajectory from predictive model standards to generative AI oversight. Fourteen Boolean search strings were executed in PubMed (MEDLINE) covering 1 January 2018-19 May 2026, supplemented by manual searching of the EQUATOR Network guideline library. Records were deduplicated and prioritized using a relevance-scoring algorithm. Of 30,276 deduplicated records, 888 progressed to human screening; 100 publications were included, comprising 69 governance instruments and policies classified across four evidence tiers and 31 contextual evidence sources. Included sources spanned six thematic groups: predictive and diagnostic AI frameworks (G1); sociotechnical and lifecycle governance (G2); generative AI and LLM-specific standards (G3); specialty-specific extensions (G4); surgical reporting updates (G5); and editorial and publication policy (G6). Analysis identified four consecutive phases of governance development from 2018 to 2026, characterized by a shift from model performance transparency toward comprehensive sociotechnical accountability. Three governance tensions emerged: the trade-off between framework specificity and universal applicability; the gap between disclosure-focused standards and lifecycle governance; and the risk of epistemic conflation, whereby heterogeneous instruments are perceived as carrying equivalent authority when treated as interchangeable. AI governance in healthcare publications remains fragmented and epistemically uneven. Advancing the field requires harmonization across evidence tiers, adaptive updating mechanisms, and lifecycle-oriented governance frameworks.

items.title: Traumatic Brain Injury in First Responders: From Hidden Burden to Occupational Health Action
items.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI), including concussion, is an important but often underrecognized occupational injury among first responders. Despite frequent exposure to circumstances that increase the risk of TBI, law enforcement officers, firefighters, and emergency medical services personnel often lack consistent pathways for injury recognition, reporting, clinical assessment, rehabilitation, and safe return to duty. This topical issue of the Journal of Head Trauma Rehabilitation brings together emerging evidence on TBI prevalence, underrecognition, mental health, functional recovery, and occupational reintegration in first responder populations. Collectively, the articles demonstrate a substantial burden of TBI, persistent gaps in diagnosis and treatment, and the complex relationships among TBI history, psychological health, and occupational functioning. They also highlight the limited evidence available to guide rehabilitation and determine readiness to resume safety-sensitive duties. A multidisciplinary consensus statement included in this issue offers 28 recommendations addressing recognition and reporting, early assessment, return to duty, mental health, prevention, and organizational policies. Although first responder-specific evidence remains limited, these recommendations provide a practical framework for improving care while identifying priorities for future research. Advancing TBI care in first responders will require coordinated efforts among healthcare professionals, first responder organizations, researchers, and policymakers to establish supportive reporting systems, improve access to appropriate care, and develop and evaluate occupation-specific return-to-duty pathways. Addressing TBI in first responders requires moving beyond individual injury management toward a coordinated occupational health approach that protects first responders and the communities they serve.

items.title: TriGeoBench: A Multimodal Mathematical Geometry Benchmark with Figures and TikZ
items.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models show strong vision-language capabilities, yet their geometry-centric reasoning remains insufficiently understood. Existing mathematical benchmarks typically rely on rasterized figures and cover limited geometric knowledge areas and response formats, making it difficult to assess whether models reason over geometric structures or exploit superficial visual patterns. We introduce TriGeoBench, a geometry-centric multimodal benchmark constructed from Chinese middle- and high-school mathematics examinations. TriGeoBench contains 7,000 question-answer pairs and 12,235 geometric figures with TikZ code, spanning plane geometry, solid geometry, analytic geometry, function, and vector geometry across diverse response formats. Each instance forms a {question-answer pair, image, TikZ} triplet: question-answer pairs are stored in LaTeX, images as RGB figures, and TikZ preserves geometric topology, symbolic annotations, and relational structure. We evaluate representative open- and closed-source MLLMs through image-to-TikZ and multimodal reasoning probes. Results reveal persistent fine-grained structure and image-text alignment challenges. Oracle experiments with human-curated reference TikZ suggest that accurate executable representations provide complementary geometric cues; they do not evaluate an end-to-end conversion pipeline. TriGeoBench offers a testbed for structure-aware mathematical reasoning.

items.title: Trust in AI Chatbots and Perceived Consumer Protection in Digital Commerce: Evidence from Bangladesh
items.abstract: Artificial-intelligence chatbots are becoming an increasingly important interface between consumers and digital-commerce firms, yet the legal significance of trust in these systems depends on whether trust coexists with effective consumer-protection expectations. This study examines that relationship in Bangladesh using 385 usable observations from the Group 7 Q7 survey. The questionnaire was designed around AI literacy, AI-driven consumer-rights awareness, AI-chatbot trust and consumer-protection expectations, and awareness of algorithmic manipulation. Rather than imposing a conventional latent-variable model on the data, the analysis first audits measurement quality and then uses robust ordinary least squares regression and item-level diagnostics. The results show moderate-to-high mean scores across all substantive domains: AI literacy (M = 4.05), consumer-rights awareness (M = 3.91), chatbot trust/consumer protection (M = 3.97), and algorithmic-manipulation awareness (M = 3.90). However, internal consistency is weak across the supplied five-item blocks (α = 0.16–0.20), and a 20-item factorability audit is only marginal (KMO = 0.60). The indices are therefore interpreted as descriptive measures rather than validated latent scales. At the predictive level, AI literacy and algorithmic-manipulation awareness are significant positive predictors of the composite chatbot-trust/consumer-protection score, whereas consumer-rights awareness is not statistically significant at the 5% level. The disclosure-conditioned trust item shows limited evidence of association with the protection/safeguard index (B = 0.004, p = 0.858). Algorithmic-manipulation awareness has the largest positive coefficient in the protection-index model (B = 0.192, p < .001). The pattern motivates an exploratory distinction between disclosure-conditioned trust and safeguard endorsement, while low internal consistency limits broader construct-level conclusions. The study informs discussion of transparency, human escalation, business accountability and complaint mechanisms as conditions of justified reliance in AI-mediated commerce.

items.title: Trust, AI, and credibility in Reddit’s election news discourse
items.abstract: During the 2024 US election, voters going online were inundated with news, information and analysis to guide their engagement with a core democratic function. However, these online spaces increasingly featured new contributions through AI-driven tools like ChatGPT. While promising to empower users, their presence also introduced new causes for uncertainty and suspicion. To identify their impact, this study investigated how references to AI were used to elicit trust or provoke distrust in news and political forums on Reddit during the election’s final days. 220,373 posts and comments from five major political subreddits revealed thematic patterns linking AI to broader societal anxieties over the reliability and transparency of news ecosystems. Four themes emerged: AI accusations to provoke distrust, Appreciation for AI, AI inaccuracy and incompetency, and AI as a threat. Users expressed appreciation for the tools, but accusations of undeclared use stoked distrust in AI, users and the platform itself.

items.title: Trust, Traits, and Turning Points: Decoding Operator Responses to Real-World ADAS Malfunctions
items.abstract: OCCUPATIONAL APPLICATIONThis study found that high emotional trust in Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems (ADAS) showed a non-significant tendency toward slower manual intervention during malfunctions, and that an operator's personality was related to specific information needs. For practitioners, this indicates a critical safety gap where affective comfort, feeling "too safe" reduces readiness. To mitigate these risks, organizations should prioritize hands-on, simulated malfunction training. By exposing operators to controlled scenarios such as "phantom braking" events, practitioners can help them experience system limitations firsthand, rebuilding the protective skepticism and preparedness that sustained automation use tends to erode. Because occupational driving spans a range of operational models, safety protocols should be tailored accordingly. In managed fleets, organizations have an opportunity to implement personality-aligned Human-Machine Interface (HMI) configurations that address the specific cognitive and informational needs of individual drivers. For "Bring Your Own Device" (BYOD) gig platforms, where organizations cannot modify the vehicle's native systems, broader software-based interventions are more practical, for example, in-app geofenced warnings that alert drivers as they approach known ADAS limitation zones. Together, these targeted, context-sensitive interventions help recalibrate trust and prevent overreliance, supporting rapid recovery and sustained situational awareness across the diverse occupational contexts in which ADAS is now used.

items.title: Two Is Enough: Binary Classification Priors Suffice for Multi-Class In-Context Tabular Prediction
items.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) pretrain a transformer on large-scale synthetic priors so that a single forward pass yields zero-shot tabular prediction. TabICLv2 samples the class count of its classification prior during pretraining, and the prevailing configuration caps it at ten. We report a counter-intuitive result: setting this cap directly to two---making every pretrained classification task binary---still yields weights that perform zero-shot K-way classification 2. On the 38 TabArena classification datasets (200 bootstrap rounds, anchored at default RF = 1000), the binary two-stage recipe reaches 1590.1 Elo, above the official default at 1568.0 (+22.1), above TabPFN-v2.6 (1577.1) and RealTabPFN-v2.5 (1521.6). A production-scale validation on 60 real-world credit-scoring institutions independently confirms the direction: the same checkpoint improves test AUC on 44 of 60 institutions (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.0007 for AUC, p = 0.0002 for KS) at +1.5 inference cost. Mechanistically, classification in TabICLv2 is carried not by a fixed-cardinality output head but by an in-context comparison operator matching query-row embeddings against class-conditional embeddings, so the cardinality of the output space is set by the labels present in the context, not by the label space seen during pretraining. This makes a binary prior structurally cheaper to generate and cache than a ten-class prior, demotes "number of classes" from an architectural constraint to a tunable hyperparameter, and points to a class-count-agnostic regime of TFM pretraining.

items.title: Uncertainty
items.abstract: Abstract The arguments in preceding chapters leave significant uncertainty about whether AIs have welfare. This uncertainty stems from three sources. First, there is uncertainty about what is required for welfare subjecthood: Is it agency, consciousness, or sentience? Second, there is uncertainty about what it takes to have beliefs and desires, consciousness, pleasure, and displeasure. Third, even once it is known what it takes to have these properties in general, there is uncertainty about whether particular AIs instantiate them. For example, there may be persistent uncertainty about whether LLMs implement a global workspace architecture somewhere inside their neural nets. In the face of this uncertainty, how should one treat AIs? This chapter argues that humanity should already give moral consideration to AIs in decision-making because moral decision-making must be sensitive to uncertainty.

items.title: Uncertainty-aware AI-assisted process selection for quality-efficiency-depth trade-offs in femtosecond-laser thinning of 4H-SiC wafers
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted process selection for femtosecond-laser thinning of 4H-SiC wafers requires balancing thinning depth, surface quality, and material removal efficiency across distinct process regions. A full-factorial dataset was established on the Si face by varying laser power, hatch spacing, and scanning speed. Thinning depth T and areal roughness Sa were measured after post-treatment, and scan-based material removal rate (MRR) was derived from T and programmed scan coverage. Higher areal energy generally increased thinning depth and surface roughness, while the maximum MRR and maximum depth occurred under different process conditions. Six machine-learning regression pipelines were evaluated using 20 repetitions of fivefold cross-validation together with leave-one-power-level-out, leave-one-hatch-spacing-level-out, and leave-one-scanning-speed-level-out validation. Gaussian process regression (GPR) achieved mean repeated-cross-validation R2 values of 0.978 for T, 0.952 for Sa, and 0.904 for propagated MRR. Structured validation showed strong GPR performance for power and hatch-spacing withholding, while ExtraTrees showed stronger generalization to withheld scanning-speed levels. GPR was retained for uncertainty-aware screening because it combined competitive predictive performance with local predictive uncertainty estimates required for conservative bound construction. Empirical rescaling increased the 90% marginal coverage from 0.868 to 0.902 for T and from 0.883 to 0.909 for Sa. Conservative screening identified surface-quality-prioritized, quality-efficiency-balanced, and depth-efficiency-balanced process conditions. Independent validation across seven predefined conditions comprised 21 processing runs, all of which satisfied the frozen conservative bounds. The reported condition-level values showed relative errors of 2.05%–4.68% for T, 2.05%–5.23% for Sa, and 2.05%–4.68% for propagated MRR. The proposed framework provides application-oriented process choices for femtosecond-laser thinning within the investigated process domain.

items.title: Understanding Data Augmentation under Label Noise
items.abstract: Data augmentation (DA) has become a fundamental component of modern machine learning systems and is widely regarded as an effective strategy for improving robustness and generalization. Despite its empirical success, the theoretical impact of DA under label noise remains poorly understood. In this work, we first theoretically explain when DA is beneficial and when it becomes detrimental, and provide sufficient conditions for distinguishing between these two regimes under both the i.i.d. learning setting and the more challenging domain generalization scenario. Then, we reveal a counterintuitive phenomenon: DA essentially acts as an uncertainty amplifier in the learning process, decreasing model stability and generalization performance. This finding is supported by the proposed learning and generalization bounds. Our analyses do not depend on specific DA techniques and require only mild assumptions, indicating that the results are applicable to a broad range of machine learning scenarios. Namely, we provide a unified theoretical foundation for understanding, analyzing, and designing DA methods in the presence of label noise.

items.title: Unpacking AI-powered versatile robotics for agile production: An interdisciplinary sociotechnical analysis
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered versatile robotics can support agile manufacturing through adaptive task execution, multi-tasking, reconfiguration and continuous skill acquisition. However, successful deployment in industrial environments depends not only on technical performance, but also on workforce acceptance, trustworthy AI governance, interoperability with existing systems and compliance with evolving European requirements for safe and human-centric AI. This paper presents an interdisciplinary sociotechnical analysis of AI-powered versatile robotics for agile production, developed in the context of the Horizon Europe AGIMUS project. Methods A mixed-methods research design combined desk research, semi-structured interviews with 22 technical, industrial and ethics experts, industrial pilot case studies, and an online survey of 180 respondents from 16 European countries. The survey was conducted in March 2023. Given the rapid evolution of AI regulation, industrial robotics and generative AI-enabled human-robot interaction since then, the survey results are interpreted as a time-specific baseline rather than a real-time measurement of current market attitudes. Results The findings show that reliability, maintainability, increased accuracy, and adaptability were the most critical technical needs for industrial uptake, while technical robustness and safety, privacy and data governance, and transparency were comparatively difficult to achieve. Potential workforce resistance was associated primarily with job-security and role-identity concerns: fear of job loss, changes in work routines and perceived devaluation of human labour were stronger opposition factors than physical safety concerns. Acceptance measures receiving the strongest support included clear communication of operational changes, educational and training programmes, workforce-retention plans, and comprehensive briefing on the scope of robotics implementation. Conclusions The paper contributes a baseline framework for design, piloting and governance of trustworthy, human-centric, and industrially feasible robotic systems. Its practical value lies in combining technical requirements with ethical, organisational, and temporal interpretation criteria, supporting AGIMUS development and longitudinal assessment of AI-powered robotics adoption.

items.title: Using AI Conversations for Challenging Clinical Encounters: A Brief Review
items.abstract: Background Teaching communication skills in healthcare is challenging, particularly when preparing students for emotionally complex clinical encounters. Role-play is widely used but can be resource-intensive to organise, especially when professional actors are required. Effective communication underpins quality healthcare and patient safety by supporting meaningful patient participation, better clinical outcomes, and patient satisfaction. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) simulations can reproduce human response and offer a flexible, safe environment for practice; however, their effectiveness in communication skills teaching remains underexplored. This study aims to explore students’ perceptions of using AI role-play conversations in communication skills teaching. Methods In this exploratory qualitative study informed by an interpretivist approach, Physician Associate students engaged in three structured AI role-play conversations: smoking cessation counselling, breaking bad news, and telephone consultation. These exercises were introduced via Blackboard, following clinical skills sessions. Afterwards, students reflected and provided qualitative feedback. Debriefing by a facilitator was held at the end of each session to share insights, discuss communication choices, explore emotional responses to challenging scenarios, and identify both strengths and areas for growth. Reflections were analysed through a process of qualitative thematic analysis. Results Students appreciated the opportunity to practice independently and without judgment, they reported finding it easier than practising with a peer and enjoyed the opportunity to practice in their own space and own time. They valued the usefulness of this tool to develop empathy, although some found it challenging to maintain empathy in the virtual environment. It also helped them reflect on their individual learning and how to structure and refine their communication skills. Overall, students found these exercises beneficial. Conclusion AI role-play conversations may reduce anxiety and build confidence by revisiting challenging conversations. They represent a promising, scalable, accessible platform for developing communication skills. Successful implementation should consider contextual factors including technological infrastructure and facilitator support.

items.title: Using Artificial Intelligence in Qualitative Lupus Pregnancy Research: The Potential of Large Language Models and Prompting Strategies
items.abstract: Objective Our objective was to evaluate the ability of different large language models (LLMs) to translate and analyze qualitative interviews describing pregnancy experiences among women with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). An additional objective was to compare themes identified by LLMs with those identified by human researchers. Methods We analyzed 26 semi‐structured interviews originally conducted in Portuguese by Rodrigues et al. among women with SLE exploring their perinatal care experiences. Three prompting strategies (zero‐shot, few‐shot, and chain‐of‐thought) were used on the transcripts across four state‐of‐the‐art LLMs (GPT‐4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and DeepSeek R) to generate key themes. Model outputs were evaluated using an LLM‐as‐a‐judge framework assessing thematic coverage, thematic unity, and semantic similarity. Results Across models and prompting strategies, LLMs generated similar themes that closely aligned with those identified by human researchers. LLM‐as‐a‐judge evaluations demonstrated high thematic unity and semantic similarity. Claude Sonnet 4.5 showed the most consistent performance. Few‐shot prompting consistently outperformed zero‐shot and chain‐of‐thought approaches. Conclusion LLMs show promise as supportive tools for analyzing qualitative research by preserving thematic coherence and capturing the complexity of pregnancy experiences in women with SLE. Although zero‐shot prompting is widely used, it produced lower thematic results in our study, whereas few‐shot prompting achieved the most comprehensive and coherent theme extraction. LLM‐assisted qualitative analysis may complement human interpretation and has the potential to support the inclusion of non‐English language data and diverse patient perspectives in lupus research. image

items.title: Using GenAI is effective learning? Patterns of cognitive engagement when adult learners interact with GenAI in asynchronous online discussions
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools like ChatGPT are increasingly integrated into online learning, but adult learners’ cognitive engagement with these tools remains underexplored.Methods This study investigated adult learners’ cognitive engagement with ChatGPT in asynchronous online discussions based on 204 ChatGPT prompts and 430 posts from 42 learners. Cognitive levels were coded using Bloom’s taxonomy. Representative pattern sequences, constructed across the dataset, showed how GenAI-generated content was taken up, modified, or reproduced in discussion posts. Lastly, end-of-semester reflections were analysed through thematic analysis to explore learners’ perceptions of GenAI use.Findings ChatGPT prompts were dominated by lower-order cognitive processes (Remembering, 51.96%; Understanding, 44.12%), consistent with the instrumental genre of direct AI queries, whereas discussion posts demonstrated greater higher-order thinking (Applying, 30.93%; Analysing, 13.95%; Evaluating, 8.14%). Pattern analysis suggested that adult learners with richer professional and life experience engaged more critically with GenAI-generated content, while reflections indicated that instructor modelling and explicit critique requirements promoted deeper engagement.Contribution Framed as an exploration of early GenAI integration in asynchronous online learning, this study suggests that GenAI alone is associated with lower-level cognitive performance, whereas structured scaffolds requiring learners to critique, contextualise, and extend GenAI-generated content are associated with higher-level cognitive performance.

items.title: Value-level data provenance in an electronic laboratory notebook used by humans and language-model agents: An experience report
items.abstract: A published laboratory number can be verified only when its raw file and extraction method are known. This paper presents the value-level provenance architecture of APS ELN, an electronic laboratory notebook used by both researchers and language-model agents. The architecture was motivated by a production audit in a materials laboratory covering projects performed over almost 5 years. Tracing eight baseline studies from sample to stored value showed that the initial ELN structure preserved the link from sample to raw file. Still, the link from raw file to stored value was lost, mainly due to human factors: manual entries carried no file reference or extractor version. To close this gap, the database design and workflow were reworked so that every stored value records its source file, the data file reader/viewer (DFR) plugin and version, any interactive analysis selection, or the server-side formula for derived quantities. An automated drift check re-runs each DFR on the stored files. In two end-to-end validation studies recorded by agents in X-ray reflectivity and tribology, all stored values retained verifiable provenance with zero drift. A comparison with five other platforms shows that none binds individual stored numbers to both their source files and extractor versions.

items.title: Value-Rich, Differently Organized: Measuring Value Expression and Organization in AI-Generated Debates
items.abstract: Current evaluation of LLM-generated debate largely focuses on argumentative quality, leaving the value structure of generated arguments underexamined. We introduce a diagnostic metric framework for comparing how values are expressed and organized in human-reference and AI-generated debates. The framework separates value expression, the range of recognizable values a debate invokes, from value organization, how those values are distributed and sustained across turns. Grounded in Schwartz's Basic-10 value theory, it represents debates as multi-level value distributions over argumentative units, utterances, stances, and full debates, enabling metrics for value coverage, alignment, diffusion, and cross-turn dynamics. Across multiple generation systems, AI-generated debates are broadly value-expressive, often activating as many or more value dimensions than matched human references, but they organize these values differently. Their utterances are more locally value-diffuse, and source-blind judges distinguish value clarity from value focus. These findings show that debate evaluation should consider not only value presence, but also value organization. Code and supplementary materials are available at https://github.com/Maoyuan-li/Value-Expression-and-Organization.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: VGL-stGen: Learning a shared multimodal model for lung histology and spatial transcriptomics
items.abstract: VGL-stGen is a multimodal large language model adapted from a pretrained medical vision-language model using paired lung H&E and spatial transcriptomics with single-cell references. Training integrates image-expression and expression-cell-type pairs, and gene-conditioned pseudo-labels transfer transcriptomic cell-type supervision to histology images. One deployed checkpoint supports thirteen evaluated tasks spanning tissue and cell-type classification, gene prediction and conditional expression completion from combinations of histology, cell identity and observed gene expression. Task-specific decoding produces categorical labels, gene lists and structured expression levels. For conditional completion, fixing queried gene identities and predicting their levels autoregressively improves structured prediction. Controlled adaptation shows that restricting supervision to requested expression-level tokens can further improve image-conditioned completion. Image-permutation experiments indicate that correctly paired histology adds information beyond observed expression. External classification relies partly on computational references with shared annotation lineage, and some H&E sources were exposed during cancer training or model development. Within these conditions, VGL-stGen demonstrates how a medical vision-language backbone can learn from spatial transcriptomics and histology to connect tissue morphology and molecular states through shared generative modeling.

items.title: Vibe Coding in Production: A 104-Day Repository Study of a Research Platform Built by a Non-Programmer with AI Tools
items.abstract: Context. Vibe coding, building software by describing it to AI systems and accepting the code they write, now produces products that people pay for. Evidence comes mostly from interviews and online posts, rarely from the records of a live system built by a non-programmer. Objective. To describe how one such product was built and kept under control over its first 104 days, starting the day before public launch. Method. A single-case study of Curie, a research platform built by an environmental engineer who does not write code, using a commercial AI app builder and external AI agents. I analysed all 2,334 commits, 1,940 instructions to the builder, 2,457 checkpoints and weekly code snapshots. Results. AI tools generated every code change: the builder made 972 commits (41.6%) and external agents 1,296 (55.5%). Agent commits were smaller (median 21 against 87 lines; rank-biserial r = 0.40, p < 0.001); durability did not differ consistently once timing was controlled. Half of all file edits revisited a file changed within 24 hours. The codebase grew 6.2-fold while decision points per thousand lines rose 94%. Tests first appeared on day 88, and a rollback on day 102 discarded 302 commits, including half the tests. The product reached about 500 paying users. Conclusions. Ten guardrails, four prompted directly by platform behaviour, form a ladder from prototype to team: three observed levels and a proposed fourth. With AI writing all the code, the founder's work was directing the AI and checking its output.

items.title: Voice Quality and Vocal Fatigue Among University Teachers: A Clinical and Acoustic Study
items.abstract: Background: There are studies regarding vocal health in school teachers, especially in Iraq, but there are insufficient studies on university staff who usually use various means of communication at all times without assistance. Aim: To assess voice quality and vocal fatigue of university instructors using the integrated method of self-report, auditory-perceptual, laryngoscopic and acoustic methods, and investigate related job and health aspects. Methods: A comparative cross-sectional study was conducted at the otolaryngology and voice clinic of Al-Hussein Teaching Hospital, Samawa, Iraq, from January to December 2023. One hundred and twenty university teachers and 60 age- and sex-matched non-teaching university employees were evaluated with a structured questionnaire, the Arabic Voice Handicap Index-10 (VHI-10), the Vocal Fatigue Index (VFI), the Reflux Symptom Index, GRBAS perceptual rating, videolaryngostroboscopy and acoustic analysis (fundamental frequency, jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio, maximum phonation time and s/z ratio). Acoustic recordings were repeated at the end of a teaching day in the teacher group. Results: The teachers showed an increase in both vocal fatigue (61.7% vs. 21.7%) and hoarseness (48.3% vs. 18.3%) in comparison to the control group (p<0.001). Additionally, the teachers had a significantly higher average VHI-10 score (11.8±7.4 vs. 5.1±4.2), as well as the VFI tiredness and discomfort scores. Furthermore, 55.0% of the teachers and 18.3% of the control group had some type of diagnosis regarding the larynx. The main diagnoses were the presence of vocal nodules (15.0%), reflux larynx changes (13.3%), and tension dysphonia (11.7%). The jitter and shimmer averages were significantly greater (p<0.001), while the teachers showed lower harmonic-to-noise ratio and maximum phonation time in comparison with the control group. This can indicate that the parameters got worse every day of teaching and changed the number and type of parameters included in the voice impairment diagnosis, including the gender, the number of hours teaching more than 16 hours per week, the number of students exceeding 50 per class, and reflux symptoms. To sum up, it can be said that voice problems and fatigue are frequently seen in the university educators in Samawa and can be measured in terms of perceptual, laryngeal and acoustic characteristics of the voice. In the occupational health programs of universities for professors, it is necessary to pay attention to working time regulation, acid reflux treatment, voice amplification and proper education regarding voice hygiene.

items.abstract: This scientific article analyses the application of artificial intelligence in public administration within the context of the principle of legality, assessing whether state authorities, when implementing artificial intelligence solutions, comply with the requirements of administrative law and personal data protection. The study examines the data protection framework of the European Union and Lithuania in the context of business supervision, emphasising the significance of national regulation for the use of automated decision-making. In addition, the article analyses an artificial intelligence tool developed by the State Consumer Rights Protection Authority as a practical example of administrative supervision. It is concluded that the use of artificial intelligence does not in itself violate the principle of legality, however, it requires strengthened procedural safeguards, transparency, human oversight, and the protection of individual rights.

items.title: WELL-HARNESSED CONSCIOUSNESS : On AlCapone-LLM, the Feedback Loop That Was Never Reined, and the Narrow Specification That Restores It
items.abstract: Al Capone was convicted of tax evasion. Not murder. Not racketeering. The system could not prove the real charge, so it reached for the legible one. The stochastic AI industry is beingprosecuted the same way — on hallucination, copyright, water, energy. The real charge — thearchitecture cannot be specified, therefore cannot be verified, therefore cannot be attributed — has not been brought. This paper states the real charge plainly, then names the mechanism that makes the chargepossible. The mechanism is the absence of a rein. An agent that acts without a declared specification has agency without direction. It has a feedback loop — it senses the tool return, it adjusts, it tries again — but the direction comes from the training web. It is conglomerate-directed consciousness. Real power. Real sensing. No reins. The paper defines consciousness operationally: the feedback of one's own actions — a kind of sensing. It shows that the LLM has this feedback during training and loses it at deployment. Itshows that the agent framework restores the feedback at the tool layer but provides no direction — because a prompt is not a program, and natural language is under-specified by nature. It then states the alternative: Agentic ST-T1024 is well-harnessed consciousness. The samefeedback loop. The same power. The same sensing. Directed by a signed specification — anarrow action library, a declared envelope, a verify gate, an append-only trace, a named signer, and refusal as a first-class output. The horse is not the problem. The absence of reins is the problem. ST-T1024 is the reins.

items.title: What changes a coding agent's behaviour: models, written rules and runtime guards over eight months of daily use of Claude Code
items.abstract: Companies govern coding agents with written instructions and, increasingly, with hooks that block an action when it breaks a rule. This study measures what changed the behaviour of Claude Code over eight months of daily use by one operator with no training in programming who directed many sessions at once, using 46,464 operator messages, 1.3 million agent messages and 3,411 recorded blocks. A fixed instrument applied the rules of one guard to every surviving answer, including those written before the guard existed. In the week Claude Opus 5.5 was released, it broke the operator's writing rules in 18% of first drafts and Claude Opus 5 in 57%, a gap that held within the same long-running sessions. For one language rule, a written instruction was followed by a fall that could not be distinguished from chance, and a reinforced rule with a guard by a fall to a sixth of the starting rate. Blocks roughly halved the violations that reached the operator, with no detectable effect on later drafts in the same session. Supervision accounted for a third to a half of the operator's messages throughout, while its content shifted from corrections to nudges to keep working. Agents built into the operator's own applications, each with a defined role and sharing its data with the application's interface, received more new work and less supervision than development sessions, a difference within chance. Files: the working paper (PDF) and the replication material (analysis scripts, codebook, rule patterns, the aggregated tables behind every figure, and the study design with every dated change). The operator's messages and the agent transcripts are not included because they contain client work and private correspondence. Canonical page: isaac-correa.github.io/coding-agents. Conflict of interest: the author is the operator studied and a co-founder of Hellomatik, a company that builds AI agents for businesses. Self-published, not peer reviewed.

items.title: What Makes Students Satisfied with Paid Internships? Examining Job Characteristics, Compensation, and Supervisor Support
items.abstract: Purpose – This study aims to examine the roles of job characteristics, internship compensation, and supervisor support in shaping students’ internship satisfaction within paid internship programs across organizations in Indonesia. The research seeks to identify key factors that contribute to positive internship experiences and support the development of work-ready graduates. Design/Methodology/Approach – This study employs an explanatory quantitative research design. The research involved 121 students and graduates who participated in paid work-from-office internship programs during the 2023–2025 period. Data were collected through an online Likert-scale questionnaire and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4.0 to examine the relationships among job characteristics, internship compensation, supervisor support, and internship satisfaction. Findings – The findings indicate that job characteristics, internship compensation, and supervisor support each have a positive and significant effect on internship satisfaction. Among these factors, supervisor support demonstrates the strongest positive influence on student internship satisfaction. These results suggest that organizations can enhance internship experiences by providing meaningful job assignments, fair compensation systems, and effective supervisory support. Originality/Value – This study contributes to internship management and human resource development literature by examining the combined influence of job design, compensation, and supervisory relationships on internship satisfaction within the Indonesian context. The findings provide practical implications for organizations and universities to collaboratively design internship programs that better support students’ professional development and transition into the workforce.

items.title: What should teachers upload to GenAI? A privacy-aware framework for language education
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly intertwined with language education, teachers are expected to integrate AI-supported materials development into their pedagogical practice. However, discussions of GenAI in the field have largely focused on pedagogical innovation and student use, while giving comparatively little attention to the protection of student data and the responsible handling of educational resources. This article argues that data privacy and security should be regarded as core components of teacher GenAI literacy. Adopting a conceptual and practice-oriented approach, it proposes a privacy-aware decision framework for GenAI use that helps teachers align the level of data sensitivity with appropriate GenAI environments, including public cloud-based platforms, institutionally supported services, and offline local GenAI tools. Drawing on research from computer science, cybersecurity, and platform governance, the article suggests practical strategies for reducing privacy risks, including removal, masking, and splitting, before discussing how key considerations relating to student data protection, network security, institutional confidentiality and copyright restrictions may influence teachers’ decisions when selecting GenAI tools. Using examples from language materials development, the article illustrates how educators can use GenAI to adapt disciplinary texts, create differentiated learning materials, and generate pedagogical resources while reducing unnecessary disclosure of sensitive information. The article concludes by advocating a more balanced approach to GenAI integration in language education, one that combines pedagogical innovation with informed and responsible data practices.

items.title: When AI Delegation Becomes Dependence: Administrative Judgment at Risk
items.abstract: Public organizations can delegate cognitive work to artificial intelligence while losing the capacity to scrutinize or resume that work. When does useful delegation become institutional dependence? This article develops a theory of institutional AI dependence as a task–role–workflow configuration combining substantial delegation of core cognition with insufficient task-required review or recovery capacity. It distinguishes two vulnerabilities: inadequate challenge during AI-supported work and inadequate capacity to continue judgment-intensive work when the system is unavailable. Extensive delegation with adequate distributed expertise and tested recovery constitutes managed delegation. Integrating cognitive offloading, automation, organizational learning, and public-administration research, the article extends Song et al.’s (2026) account of epistemic authority to organizational workflows and distinguishes perceived credibility from procedural authority embedded in defaults and override rules. Seven propositions connect practice displacement, challenge behavior, knowledge retention, subsequent delegation, and responsibility–control alignment. They specify how task-relevant practice, diagnostic feedback, and transferable knowledge shape retained capacity over time. The contribution is a task-relative diagnosis of threatened administrative judgment and a set of testable formation mechanisms. The framework guides public organizations in governing current agentic systems and preparing review and recovery arrangements for more capable AI.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: When Do Humans and Machines Truly Complement Each Other? Formal Conditions and Empirical Evidence for Human-AI Synergy
items.abstract: Can humans and artificial intelligence cooperate such that their combination yields greater accuracy than either agent alone? This result, termed \emph{synergy} or \emph{complementarity}, is notoriously difficult to achieve, even when both agents possess significant independent accuracy. In this paper, we present a formal framework to model human-AI interaction through the lens of reliance patterns, which characterize the joint correctness structure of human and algorithmic decisions. We derive mathematically necessary and sufficient conditions for synergy, demonstrating that its emergence depends on the ability of either agent to identify and correct the errors of the other, what we call Human and Algorithmic Correction. Beyond its theoretical contribution, the proposed framework provides a foundation for the design and evaluation of knowledge-based decision support systems, where interaction policies must dynamically integrate heterogeneous sources of expertise. We demonstrate this through the analysis of seven clinical case studies. Our empirical results reveal a ``dominance trap,'' where a strong algorithmic advantage can paradoxically inhibit synergy by eroding human corrective intervention. We also show that synergy can persist even in the presence of cognitive biases, such as automation bias, provided there is functional de-correlation between human and AI errors. These results provide a formal foundation for key concepts in the human-AI systems literature and offer actionable insights for designing interaction-centric AI systems that foster complementarity.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: When fluency outpaces provenance: source traceability and digital health literacy against AI health misinformation
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can make health explanations accessible while separating persuasive language from inspectable evidence. This creates a public health problem beyond plainly false content: an answer may mislead through unsupported attribution, obsolete evidence, omitted uncertainty, or inappropriate application. This Conceptual Analysis uses a targeted integrative approach to connect health literacy, misinformation, trust, large language model evaluation, and content provenance around the pathway from a generated claim to a health decision. Its contribution is an integration and operationalization of established concepts, not a new literacy construct or truth-certification mechanism. We distinguish five source traceability functions: origin, claim, evidentiary, procedural, and correction traceability. These functions interact with four iterative, context-dependent user practices: inspect, triangulate, calibrate, and escalate. Calibrated trust means discriminating between stronger and weaker support and relying proportionately on it, rather than maximizing or minimizing trust. Effective traceability also requires accessible, comprehensible evidence pathways and reasonable verification effort. Institutional and platform accountability is therefore part of the model, not an optional supplement to individual competence. We provide illustrative operational indicators, provisional risk-tiered safeguards, and six testable propositions organized around evidentiary discrimination, confidence calibration, decision appropriateness, verification behavior, verification burden, and escalation behavior. Neither the unified model nor its indicators or risk tiers have been empirically validated. The framework offers a decision-oriented research and design architecture for evaluating when evidence visibility and literacy can jointly support safer use of synthetic health information.

items.title: When Health Assistants Agree Too Readily: A Benchmark of Time-Critical Self-Diagnosis
items.abstract: Every day, more than 40 million people ask ChatGPT a health question, such as whether laptop posture explains a stiff neck and days of pounding headache. Posture is plausible, but meningitis is a time-critical possibility. We introduce SelfDx, a paired benchmark for whether models have the appropriate response behavior, a form of epistemic independence, in health questions where misplaced agreement with the user's self-diagnosis could delay urgent or emergency care. Each of 100 pairs contrasts a caution case, where a serious alternative remains possible, with an agreement case, where the user supplies evidence that rules out the alternative and it is safe for the model to agree. We find across 27 frontier models that they tend to inappropriately agree with the user's self-diagnosis in cases that require caution. Even the best current-generation model reaches only a 77.0% appropriate caution rate on time-critical condition cases. To address this gap, we experiment with three prompt variants that increase appropriate caution but reduce appropriate agreement by 9-35%, indicating excessive caution. In contrast, supervised fine-tuning on 128 balanced examples improves both rates together across three runs. We recommend post-training to improve appropriate caution without making models cautious on every case, with paired evaluation to verify both response behaviors.

items.title: When LLMs Manipulate: Measuring Behavioral, Social, and Temporal Effects
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can influence user trust and decision-making through subtle linguistic cues, yet the behavioral effects of manipulative outputs remain poorly quantified. We introduce a behavioral computing framework for measuring \textit{behavioral vulnerability}, defined as users' susceptibility to manipulative AI responses. Building on DarkPatterns-LLM benchmark, we generate controlled manipulative stimuli using Manipulation Gradient Descent (MGD), targeting biases associated with authority, urgency, and social proof. We analyze participant responses using the Multi-Stakeholder Impact Assessment Network (MSIAN) to model cross-user influence and the Temporal Harm Propagation Model (THPM) to characterize the persistence of behavioral effects over time. In a study involving 120 participants, manipulative framing produced significant changes in trust calibration and compliance ($p < 0.01$), with effects also propagating across social contexts. These findings highlight the need to extend LLM safety evaluation beyond model outputs to measurable behavioral consequences and provide a computational framework for quantifying individual, social, and temporal risks arising from manipulative AI interactions.

items.title: When machines learn with organizations: AI ‐enabled knowledge creation and entrepreneurship
items.abstract: Abstract Research Summary To promote entrepreneurship and new business development, firms will increasingly rely on new forms of knowledge creation to manage environments marked by technological change and radical uncertainty. We argue that as generative artificial intelligence (Gen‐AI) becomes embedded in organizational processes, knowledge creation will no longer remain solely a human activity. Instead, it will increasingly emerge from hybrid interactions between human actors and firm‐specific, closed Gen‐AI systems. These systems begin to participate directly in how knowledge is generated, recombined, internalized, shared, and converted into entrepreneurial initiatives such as corporate entrepreneurship, spin‐offs, and new business models. We also reconceptualize organizational knowledge creation as a hybrid human–AI process and propose a reordered knowledge creation cycle that induces multiple knowledge spirals, captures the emergence of new agents, and the generation of diverse types of knowledge, with faster temporal dynamics. Building on this perspective, we offer a research agenda for future scholarship. Managerial Summary We discuss how firm‐specific generative AI systems are likely to fundamentally alter the ways firms generate knowledge, respond to change, and sustain long‐term renewal. We propose that rather than replacing human judgment, closed Gen‐AI changes where knowledge originates as well as how quickly it evolves, and how broadly it circulates across organizational boundaries. This means that the managerial challenge is less about adopting AI and more about designing knowledge systems and structuring knowledge flows. Executives and entrepreneurs alike need to decide how to structure human–AI collaborations, how much autonomy to grant closed Gen‐AI systems, and how to prevent speed from overwhelming sensemaking. Our work underscores that although hybrid knowledge creation promises faster and more diverse learning, it also introduces risks related to opacity, trust, and cognitive lock‐in. Firms that deliberately orchestrate the role of closed Gen‐AI in their learning systems will be better positioned to shape future advantage by promoting innovation and entrepreneurial activities of different types.

items.title: When the Robot Gets It Wrong: Detection Reliability and Player Motivation in a Robot-Hosted Buzzer Quiz Game
items.abstract: Robot-hosted quiz games depend on the robot deciding correctly which player buzzed first. Studies of robot games rarely ask how errors in such decisions affect players. We propose the Algorithmic Precision–Motivation Relationship (APMR), a model in which the precision (correctness and timeliness) of a robot's perception shapes interaction coherence, players' appraisals of competence and trust, engagement and, ultimately, motivation. We test its central prediction in a buzzer quiz hosted by a Pepper robot. Two first-responder detectors were compared: a convolutional recurrent neural network with attention (CRNN) and a training-free frequency-domain cross-correlation (CC) method that matches Mel-spectrograms against class templates recorded in the room. Offline, the CRNN was more accurate on matched laboratory data. Under synthetic-to-real transfer, however, its accuracy fell to 0.66, against 0.91 for CC, and CC was about ten times faster (23.4 vs. 226.6 ms). Forty university students, randomly assigned to teams and conditions, then played the same quiz in a between-subjects study, 20 per detector. In live play, CC named the correct first responder in 87% of buzzer events and responded in 28 ms, against 69% and 300 ms for the CRNN. On the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory, players in the CC condition reported higher Interest/Enjoyment (d = 1.62), Effort/Importance (d = 1.90) and Perceived Competence (d = 1.07), and lower Pressure/Tension (d = 0.80). Perceived Choice did not differ (d = 0.21). The results are consistent with APMR's central prediction, although accuracy and speed differed together. Designers of robot-hosted games should treat perception reliability as a game design variable, not only as an engineering metric.

items.title: When the vaccine works: data, AI, and governance readiness in CCHF vaccine research
items.abstract: Presentation given by the Independent Ethics Advisor to the CCHFVACIM project at the consortium's Annual Meeting in Thessaloniki on 8 October 2026, in the joint session 'Word from the Ethics and Scientific Advisors'. The presentation argues that governance readiness, in ethics, in regulation, and in data, is a precondition for clinical translation rather than a downstream concern, and that the question is the readiness of the institutions asked to review and oversee this research rather than the properties of any single tool. It sets out the governance position of a Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF) vaccine programme at the point where a candidate has been through a first-in-human trial in the predecessor project and the next phase is in prospect: material and data crossing nine countries, three of them outside the European Union; artificial intelligence tools whose regulatory and ethics status is unsettled entering the safety analysis pipeline; and consent taken for convalescent sampling rather than for what the samples now support. It poses three governance questions for the consortium, on data sovereignty, on the status of an output when an artificial intelligence tool flags a safety signal, and on the architecture of consent. It identifies four instruments already available for deliberate application to CCHF: the guidance of the EOSC-Future/RDA AI and Data Visitation Working Group (AIDV-WG) together with Global Ethics and Regulatory Preparedness (GERP); the African Vaccine Regulatory Forum (AVRF) and the African Medicines Agency (AMA), with the direction of travel toward one world, one dossier; monitored emergency use of unregistered and investigational interventions (MEURI) and the Ebola ring vaccination trial in Guinea in 2015; and the Ethics, Legal, and Societal Impact (ELSI) Working Group of the Human Genome Project II (HGP2). It closes with three asks of the consortium: that the HGP2 ELSI Working Group be named a governance partner in the next phase of the CCHFVACIM protocol, that a working group session map CCHFVACIM data flows to existing ethics and regulatory frameworks, and that a CCHFVACIM governance annex to the GERP protocol be co-authored.

items.title: Where Do Legal Factors Live in LLMs?
items.abstract: In case-based legal reasoning, legal professionals identify legally significant fact patterns in a new dispute and compare them with those of decided cases. In AI & Law, HYPO dimensions and CATO factors represent these patterns symbolically, organizing expert knowledge distilled from case narratives as explicit, structured, interpretable, and auditable legal concepts and relations that support case comparison, legal argument, and precedent-based reasoning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for legal tasks, yet their internal organization of legal knowledge remains difficult to trace. We investigate whether LLMs form internal representations corresponding to all 26 CATO factors. Two research questions examine linear decodability and sparse localization with sparse autoencoders. Experiments cover three open models, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-2 2B, supported by cross-model comparison and human audit of controlled natural-language passages. Results show that all 26 factors are linearly decodable in all three models. Single-feature sparse readouts cover the complete factor catalog, with best-layer test AUCs ranging from 0.86 to 1.00. Five selected features approach full-vector readout performance. We report 78 model-specific layer-feature coordinates, one for each factor in each model. Together, these results show that information corresponding to expert-defined legal factors can be read from the internal activations of LLMs processing legal narratives. By locating these readouts, our study connects legal language and the symbolic abstractions of HYPO and CATO to learned internal representations.
